kepler-third.name: Kepler's third law
kepler-third.oneLiner: The higher the orbit, the slower the revolution
kepler-third.description: The square of the orbital period is proportional to the cube of the orbital radius. Planets, moons, and artificial satellites all obey this law.
kepler-third.significance: By setting out the regularity of planetary motion mathematically it laid the ground for Newtonian mechanics, and it is central to the analysis of exoplanet and satellite orbits.

T.description: The time it takes the satellite to go once around the Earth

T^2.description: The quantity proportional to the cube of the orbital radius

4pi2.description: A constant coming out of the geometry of a circular orbit, ≈ 39.48

G.description: The fundamental constant setting the strength of gravity. Because this number is so extremely small, everyday gravity is only noticeable when a mass as huge as the Earth is involved

M.description: The heavier the central body, the harder it pulls on the satellite. At the same orbital radius around Jupiter, the period would be far shorter

a.description: The distance between the satellite and the centre of the Earth. Because it enters cubed, even a small change moves the period a lot

a^3.description: Why raising the orbit only a little makes the period much longer

effects.description: Low Earth orbit (LEO). Gravity is strong here, so a satellite has to move fast to keep from falling. One lap every 90 minutes, and 16 sunrises a day.
Medium orbit. Gravity is weaker, so a slower orbit is enough. GPS satellites go round exactly twice a day.
Near geostationary orbit. Going round exactly once every 24 hours makes a satellite look fixed in the sky from the ground, which is why it is used for TV relays.
High orbit. Out near the Moon, the Earth's gravity is much weaker. The Moon takes as long as 27 days to go round once.

constraints.message: Anything smaller than the Earth's radius (6,371km) is inside the Earth, so no orbit is possible
Below an altitude of 200km, atmospheric drag decays the orbit quickly

milestones.label: ISS orbit
milestones.description: Altitude 400km. One lap every 90 minutes, 16 sunrises a day

milestones.label: GPS orbit
milestones.description: Altitude 20,200km. A period of exactly 12 hours

milestones.label: Geostationary orbit
milestones.description: Altitude 35,786km. Exactly 24 hours — it looks fixed in the sky

milestones.label: The Moon
milestones.description: A period of 27.3 days. The closest celestial body to Earth

ranges.template: About {ratio} times the cruising altitude of an airliner (10km)
A height of about {ratio} times the Seoul-Busan distance ({ref}km)
About {ratio} times the diameter of the Earth ({ref}km)

realWorldExamples: Calculating the mass of the Sun from the Earth's orbital period and radius
Estimating the size of an exoplanet's orbit from its observed period
Choosing a satellite's orbital altitude to give the period you want

hubble-law.name: Hubble's law
hubble-law.oneLiner: The law of cosmic expansion: the recession speed of a distant galaxy is proportional to its distance
hubble-law.description: Hubble's law states that the farther away a galaxy is, the faster it is moving away from us, with the recession speed directly proportional to the distance. The constant of proportionality, the Hubble constant, is the expansion rate of the universe and plays a key part in estimating its age. It is one of the strongest observational pieces of evidence for Big Bang cosmology.
hubble-law.significance: By showing observationally that the universe is expanding, it set modern cosmology on its way.

v.description: The speed at which the galaxy is moving away from the observer. Units: km/s.

H_0.description: The present expansion rate of the universe. About 70 km/s/Mpc.

d.description: The distance from the observer to the galaxy. Units: megaparsecs (Mpc).

realWorldExamples: Estimating distance from the redshift of a galaxy
Calculating the age of the universe (about 13.8 billion years)
Research into whether cosmic expansion is accelerating

schwarzschild-radius.name: Schwarzschild radius
schwarzschild-radius.oneLiner: The formula for the critical radius at which an object becomes a black hole
schwarzschild-radius.description: The Schwarzschild radius is the smallest radius to which an object of a given mass must be compressed to become a black hole. Squeeze the mass inside this radius and an event horizon forms, from which not even light can escape. It comes out of the Schwarzschild solution of general relativity.
schwarzschild-radius.significance: By defining the size of a black hole quantitatively, it established a central concept of relativistic astrophysics.

r_s.description: The radius of the event horizon. Units: metres (m).

G.description: The constant of universal gravitation. About 6.674×10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg².

M.description: The mass of the body. Units: kg.

c.description: The speed of light in a vacuum. About 3×10⁸ m/s.

c^2.role: Square of the speed of light
c^2.description: Sitting in the denominator, it makes the radius grow with the mass.

realWorldExamples: Calculating the Schwarzschild radius of the Sun (about 3km)
Estimating the size of the event horizon of a supermassive black hole
Analysing the critical condition for a neutron star to collapse into a black hole

stefan-boltzmann.name: Stefan-Boltzmann law
stefan-boltzmann.oneLiner: The law that a star's total radiated luminosity is proportional to the square of its radius and the fourth power of its surface temperature
stefan-boltzmann.description: The Stefan-Boltzmann law states that the total energy radiated by a black body (its luminosity) is proportional to its surface area and to the fourth power of its surface temperature. For a star, knowing the radius and the surface temperature gives the total luminosity, and conversely the luminosity and temperature let you estimate the star's size.
stefan-boltzmann.significance: By quantifying how a star's physical properties — size, temperature, and luminosity — relate, it became the basis of stellar classification and evolution theory.

L.description: The total energy the star radiates per unit time. Units: watts (W).

R.description: The radius of the star. Units: metres (m).

R^2.description: The factor proportional to the surface area (4πR²).

T.description: The effective temperature of the star's surface. Units: kelvin (K).

T^4.description: Double the temperature and the luminosity goes up 16-fold. A strongly non-linear relation.

realWorldExamples: Estimating a star's radius from its surface temperature and luminosity
Comparing the sizes of red giants and white dwarfs
Reading a star's position on the HR (Hertzsprung-Russell) diagram

wien-displacement.name: Wien's displacement law
wien-displacement.oneLiner: The law that the wavelength of peak black-body radiation is inversely proportional to temperature
wien-displacement.description: Wien's displacement law states that the wavelength at which a black body radiates most strongly is inversely proportional to its temperature. The hotter the body, the shorter the peak wavelength and the bluer it looks; the cooler it is, the longer the wavelength and the redder it shifts. The law lets you estimate a star's surface temperature from its colour alone.
wien-displacement.significance: By revealing the quantitative relation between a star's colour and its temperature, it provided the basis for spectroscopic observation of celestial objects.

\\lambda_{max}.description: The wavelength of greatest intensity in the black-body radiation spectrum. Units: metres (m).

T.description: The absolute temperature of the black body. Units: kelvin (K).

realWorldExamples: Estimating a star's surface temperature from its colour (blue stars are hot, red stars cool)
Measuring the Sun's surface temperature (about 5,778K, in the yellow part of the spectrum)
Observing cold objects with an infrared telescope

drake-equation.name: Drake equation
drake-equation.oneLiner: A probabilistic equation estimating the number of intelligent civilisations in our galaxy we could communicate with
drake-equation.description: The Drake equation estimates, as a product of several probability factors, the number of civilisations in our galaxy currently sending radio signals we could detect. The factors run from the rate of star formation to the lifetime of a civilisation, and although most of the values are uncertain, the equation lays out the search for extraterrestrial intelligence (SETI) systematically.
drake-equation.significance: By putting the search for extraterrestrial intelligence on a systematic scientific footing, it gave SETI research its theoretical framework.

N.description: The number of civilisations in the galaxy currently sending detectable signals.

R_*.description: How many new stars are born in the galaxy each year.

f_p.description: The fraction of stars that have planetary systems.

n_e.description: The number of planets in the habitable zone per planetary system.

f_l.description: The probability that life actually appears on a habitable planet.

f_i.description: The probability that life evolves into intelligent beings.

f_c.description: The probability that intelligent life develops technology that sends detectable signals.

L.description: How long a contactable civilisation goes on emitting signals. Units: years.

realWorldExamples: Setting search strategy in SETI projects
Updating the values of f_p and n_e with exoplanet discovery data
Quantitative discussion of the Fermi paradox (why we see no sign of alien civilisations)

gravitational-lensing.name: Gravitational lensing
gravitational-lensing.oneLiner: The formula for the angle by which a massive body bends the path of light
gravitational-lensing.description: Gravitational lensing is the bending of light that passes near a very massive body, caused by the curvature of spacetime. The deflection angle is proportional to the body's mass and inversely proportional to how close the light passes to it. It is a direct prediction of general relativity, first confirmed by observation during the solar eclipse of 1919.
gravitational-lensing.significance: It was the first phenomenon to confirm general relativity observationally, and it is now a key tool for mapping the distribution of dark matter.

\\theta.description: The angle by which the light is bent. Units: radians (rad).

G.description: The constant of universal gravitation. About 6.674×10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg².

M.description: The mass of the body that bends the light. Units: kg.

c.description: The speed of light in a vacuum. About 3×10⁸ m/s.

c^2.role: Square of the speed of light
c^2.description: The factor carrying the relativistic correction.

b.description: How close the light passes to the lensing body. Units: metres (m).

realWorldExamples: Observing the distorted images of background galaxies produced by a galaxy cluster
Searching for exoplanets by gravitational microlensing
Mapping the distribution of dark matter

escape-velocity.name: Escape velocity
escape-velocity.oneLiner: The formula for the minimum speed needed to break free of a body's gravity
escape-velocity.description: Escape velocity is the smallest speed an object at the surface of a body must have to leave its gravitational grip entirely. The more massive the body and the smaller its radius, the higher the escape velocity. At the Schwarzschild radius the escape velocity reaches the speed of light, which ties it directly to the definition of a black hole.
escape-velocity.significance: It underlies many problems in astrophysics, from rocket launches to whether a planet can hold on to an atmosphere and the conditions for black hole formation.

v_e.description: The minimum speed needed to leave the gravitational field. Units: m/s.

G.description: The constant of universal gravitation. About 6.674×10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg².

M.description: The mass of the body being escaped from. Units: kg.

r.description: The distance from the centre of the body to the starting point. Units: metres (m).

realWorldExamples: Calculating the Earth's escape velocity (about 11.2 km/s)
Explaining the Moon's lack of an atmosphere by its low escape velocity
The link between Jupiter's high escape velocity and its thick atmosphere
